Tony Kushner. The American playwright whose Angels in America stands as one of the most significant theatrical works of the late twentieth century and remains the most important American play of its era.

Born in 1956 in Louisiana and New Jersey, Kushner grew up around artists and politically engaged parents. His work would inherit both aesthetics and activism from them. Angels in America: A Gay Fantasia on National Themes premiered regionally in 1990. Part One, called Millennium Approaches, opened on Broadway in 1993. Part Two, Perestroika, opened the following year. This is an epic drama in two parts, encompassing the AIDS crisis, Cold War politics, and American spiritual crisis all at once.

The play won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama in 1993. It won multiple Tony Awards. In 2003, Mike Nichols adapted it as an HBO miniseries that extended its cultural reach beyond the theater into millions of homes. But the real reach of Angels in America was its subject matter and its visibility. Kushner was openly gay, and his play centers LGBTQ characters and experiences during the catastrophic early years of the AIDS pandemic, during a time when the government and media largely ignored these communities or condemned them.

The play defies easy categorization. It integrates realistic character drama with surrealism, mime, rapid scene shifts, and fantastical visitations. Kushner calls it a gay fantasia, and that title captures something essential: the technique matches the disorientation of crisis. The play follows four people during the Reagan administration. Prior Walter is living with AIDS. His lover is Louis. Joe Pitt is a conservative lawyer. Harper is his wife. These four people's lives intersect and fracture as the nation itself fractures.

And an angel appears. Not metaphorically, but actually. The angel visits Prior in his apartment. The play's spectacle and its spiritual vision coexist with material suffering and political indifference. Kushner's dialogue combines heightened language, humor, and brutal honesty. The play moves between domestic realism and epic theatrical ambition so fluidly that the contrast becomes the point.

What Kushner proved with Angels in America is that theater remains a viable medium for political engagement. LGBTQ representation on the mainstream stage had never been attempted at this scale or with this ambition. He showed that an American play could rival European modernism in formal innovation and intellectual depth. Angels in America remains the most significant American play of the late twentieth century because it did what great art does: it made visible what society wanted to ignore.
